Buchanan (Citation2017) shows that the security dilemma operates with particular force in network intrusion, since access acquired for defensive purposes is indistinguishable, from the target’s side, from preparation for attack. An experimental study by Horowitz and Lin-Greenberg (Citation2022) underscores how the presence of AI can alter human decision-making in conflict scenarios. Their findings suggest that AI can in some cases restrain decision-makers, for instance by inducing caution when it provides intelligence, and in other cases heighten escalatory pressures, for instance by provoking greater anger over an AI-caused accident. Notably, some analysts contend that the “AI arms race” trope is somewhat misleading. Scharre (Citation2021) argues that while the U.S. and China are undoubtedly competing in AI, this competition does not neatly fit the classic arms race model of rapid, quantitative buildups. What this scholarship has not yet specified is how AI-enabled systems generate escalation risk through the networks and data on which they depend, which is where the present article concentrates.¶ 2.4. Gaps and contribution¶ Awareness of AI’s implications for strategic stability is growing, but gaps remain in theory and evidence. Much of the existing literature is theoretical or anticipatory. Foundational deterrence models assume rational human decision-makers (Powell Citation1990), and how those models translate when parts of assessment and response are delegated to algorithms remains underdeveloped. Empirical work is also at an early stage. Because there have been no direct great-power conflicts involving AI, studies have relied on wargames, surveys, and simulations rather than observed state behavior. Quantitative and experimental work provides initial insight (Horowitz and Lin-Greenberg Citation2022) while leaving open how decision-making institutions in Beijing and Washington are preparing to manage crisis escalation, signaling, and command judgment when AI-enabled systems shape the information and time constraints under which leaders operate. The effect of AI on signaling and bargaining behavior is similarly underexplored, since traditional crisis signaling mechanisms may not translate cleanly to a world of automated decision loops.¶ A further gap concerns the relationship between the two literatures reviewed above. Work on cyber conflict has established that intrusion, ambiguity, and contested information generate escalation risk in their own right (Buchanan Citation2017; Futter Citation2018). Work on military AI has concentrated on autonomy and speed. The connection between them has received less attention, even though AI-enabled systems are unusually dependent on the networks and data that cyber operations target. One consequence is that assessments of military AI often treat system reliability as a technical property of the system, leaving out the adversary who has an interest in contesting it.¶ This paper addresses these gaps through a structured reading of U.S.-China strategic interaction under the shadow of AI. Rather than relying on abstract models or purely quantitative data, it uses structured case illustrations drawn from publicly available doctrines, strategy documents, and authoritative assessments to examine how AI-enabled military systems could shape crisis escalation and signaling between Washington and Beijing. The case illustrations are analytic probes, not claims about observed crisis behavior. They are used to identify how AI-enabled capabilities can (1) increase operational uncertainty through autonomy and system opacity, (2) distort or clarify signals through ISR and information processing, and (3) compress decision time, and how cyber exposure conditions each of these effects. The contribution is a bounded one. By tracing how official and quasi-official institutional outputs frame risks, thresholds, and control assumptions, the article contributes limited but policy-relevant inferences about crisis management problems created by military AI adoption.¶ 3. Conceptual foundations and causal mechanisms¶ This section sets out the concepts the analysis relies on and specifies the three mechanisms through which military AI competition may affect crisis stability between the United States and China. It defines strategic stability, crisis escalation, and risk perception, then situates the AI arms race and the concept of cyber exposure that runs through the argument. The three mechanisms follow: operational uncertainty and attribution ambiguity, signal clarity and data integrity, and decision acceleration and delegation. A final subsection specifies the conditions that determine how strongly each mechanism operates.¶ 3.1. Core concepts¶ Strategic stability traditionally refers to a state of affairs in which no party has an incentive to use nuclear weapons or escalate a conflict first, because each side remains confident in its ability to retaliate. Boulanin (Citation2019) defines it as a condition where countries are confident their adversaries “would not be able to undermine their nuclear deterrent capability using nuclear, conventional, cyber or other unconventional means” (p. 4). The inclusion of cyber means in that definition is significant for the present argument, since it acknowledges that confidence in a deterrent can be eroded without any change in the physical balance of forces. The concept emerged from Cold War nuclear strategy and encompasses both crisis stability, meaning the absence of incentives to initiate nuclear use in a crisis, and arms race stability, meaning the absence of incentives to build up armaments rapidly. In the contemporary U.S.-China context it involves nuclear forces alongside advanced conventional and AI-enabled systems that could affect the perceived balance of power. If AI technologies erode confidence in second-strike capabilities or defense postures, strategic stability weakens and the risk of confrontation rises.¶ Crisis escalation refers to the process by which a military or diplomatic confrontation grows in intensity, scope, or severity, potentially spiraling from minor incidents to full-scale conflict. Escalation can be deliberate or inadvertent. Deliberate escalation is a conscious decision to intensify pressure, while inadvertent escalation results from miscalculation, miscommunication, or accidents. Managing escalation requires clear communication, accurate perceptions of the adversary’s intentions, and reliable control over one’s own military systems, whether human or automated (Jervis Citation1976). Work since the Cold War emphasizes that misperceptions or false alarms in a crisis can provoke overreactions (Snyder and Diesing Citation1977). The mechanisms developed below concern inadvertent escalation, since that is where AI-enabled systems and their cyber exposure bear most directly.¶ Risk perception is the subjective judgment by decision-makers of the likelihood and consequences of adverse events. It shapes how leaders respond to ambiguous situations and new technologies. AI can alter these judgments in opposing directions. Decision-support tools that present confident assessments may lower the perceived risk of confrontation, while uncertainty about whether a system has been manipulated may raise it. If Chinese analysts believe U.S. AI military systems are prone to error or unpredictable behavior, they may treat routine encounters as riskier and react at lower thresholds of provocation. Misperception, the related concept, refers to a leadership misinterpreting the other side’s intentions or actions (Jervis Citation1976). Stable deterrence relies on both sides perceiving the risks of aggression accurately, so distortion in either direction is destabilizing.¶ 3.2. The AI arms race and cyber exposure¶ The term “AI arms race” describes the competitive pursuit of artificial intelligence capabilities by rival states seeking military advantage. Commentators have framed U.S.-China relations in these terms since the mid-2010s (Zwetsloot, Toner, and Ding Citation2018). The framing implies a rapid competition in which each side commits resources to AI research and deployment out of fear that falling behind would threaten national security. Some argue the metaphor misleads, since many military AI developments are incremental or dual-use and an unchecked race would be dangerous for both sides (Zwetsloot, Toner, and Ding Citation2018). For present purposes the term refers to the dynamic in which Washington and Beijing each seek to outpace the other in autonomous systems, AI-driven intelligence analysis, and decision-support tools, and in which each side’s adoption choices shape the other’s threat perceptions. As one Chinese analysis notes, the U.S. military’s pursuit of AI, including the Pentagon’s Third Offset strategy, has already prompted China to respond in kind (Ding and Jiang Citation2025). The framing underscores the competitive anxiety involved, which can exacerbate misperception and reduce willingness to cooperate on risk-reducing measures.¶ Cyber exposure is used here to describe the degree to which an AI-enabled military capability depends on data and communication links that an adversary can observe or manipulate. It is a property of the deployment, not of the model. Two systems with identical performance under test conditions can carry very different cyber exposure depending on how their data is collected, where inference runs, and how their outputs reach a commander. This bears on stability in ways that recur through the mechanisms below. Confidence in a system’s output becomes contingent on assumptions about an adversary’s access to the data behind it. Intrusion is ambiguous, since access for collection and access for disruption appear identical from the target’s side (Buchanan Citation2017). And the incentive to compromise an adversary’s AI grows as that adversary comes to rely on it, so successful integration generates its own targeting pressure.¶ 3.3. Mechanism one: operational uncertainty and attribution ambiguity¶ The first mechanism concerns the operational uncertainty created by autonomous and AI-enabled systems.
As the United States and China

. Machine learning algorithms are often described as black boxes, since their processing is difficult to interpret even for their operators. In tense scenarios this opacity can

. A drone deviating from its expected course because of a software fault may be mistaken for a deliberate intrusion.¶ Cyber exposure adds a further layer to this problem. Where a system’s sensors and links are contested, an anomaly admits of at least three readings. It may be a fault in the system, it may be adversary interference with the data or the link, or it may be a deliberate act by the operator. Distinguishing among these requires forensic access that is unavailable during a crisis and often unavailable afterwards. The attribution difficulty familiar from cyber conflict (Lindsay Citation2015) therefore appears inside the operation of AI-enabled platforms, and not only in the aftermath of an incident. The state that experiences the anomaly must decide how to respond without knowing which explanation applies, and the state that did not cause it cannot readily demonstrate that it did not.¶ Scholars warn that AI technologies

A false positive from an AI-backed early-warning system could push leadership to raise alert levels or pre-delegate launch authority, prompting countermoves.

(Aguirre, Javorsky, and Tegmark Citation2023).¶ 3.4. Mechanism two: signal clarity and data integrity¶ The second mechanism concerns the effect of AI-enhanced ISR on signal clarity. States signal intent through deployments and actions while interpreting those of others through intelligence, so stability depends on accurate interpretation and sufficient transparency to prevent false alarms.¶ AI can improve ISR capabilities. Machine learning processes satellite imagery, radar returns, and communications far faster than human analysts, enabling near-real-time detection of troop movements or missile launches. Greater visibility may reduce miscalculation by giving both sides a clearer view of the other’s posture. Reliable monitoring of Chinese nuclear forces by the United States, and the reverse, might reduce fears of a surprise strike, bolstering crisis stability (Horowitz and Scharre Citation2018), and some analysts suggest AI-enhanced ISR could improve risk assessment and the credibility of signaling among nuclear states (Boulanin Citation2019).¶ That stabilizing effect is conditional on the integrity of the underlying data, and the condition is not automatically met. An ISR pipeline is itself a target. Sensor feeds can be spoofed, training data can be corrupted, and models can be probed for the inputs that produce misclassification. Where such techniques succeed, the failure is silent. The system goes on producing confident assessments, and produces them faster than the analytic processes that once caught such errors. Transparency in this setting can be more dangerous than opacity, since a commander who distrusts a sensor will seek corroboration while a commander who trusts a compromised one will not. The deception logic that Gartzke and Lindsay (Citation2015) identify in cyberspace applies with particular force here, because systems optimized to find patterns can be fed patterns.¶ Uneven visibility compounds the problem. If one side gains a surveillance advantage it has reason to conceal that fact, which means the other may act on assumptions about its own concealment that no longer hold. China might believe its submarines remain undetected while U.S. systems have already located them. Disinformation operates at the same point in the chain, since synthetic media and false alerts injected into intelligence channels distort perceptions at the point of interpretation, well downstream of where the signal was sent. In an AI arms race, the volume of data and the reliance on algorithms to filter it may leave signals harder to read than before.¶ 3.5. Mechanism three: decision acceleration and delegation¶ The third mechanism involves the acceleration of decision-making and the compression of response windows. AI-enhanced military systems promise rapid data processing, target identification, and real-time updating of assessments. As both states integrate AI into command and control, operational tempo may increase sharply. Speed offers advantages, and it also shortens the window for human judgment, deliberation, and de-escalation.¶ Accelerating the observe-orient-decide-act cycle reduces the time available to assess threats and make strategic choices. If one side’s systems operate at machine speed, the other may feel pressure to respond in kind by delegating more authority to algorithms. The U.S. National Security Commission on AI warns that such systems “will likely increase the pace and automation of warfare across the board, reducing the time and space available for de-escalatory measures” (NSCAI Citation2021, 97).¶ Automation of response tends to follow automation of detection. Systems that autonomously launch interceptors or execute network defense measures may act before human operators can intervene. A misclassification could trigger a response, and where opposing systems react to one another, an exchange could unfold within seconds without deliberate human intent. Even short of full automation, compressed timelines can induce premature decisions based on incomplete information, since leaders may act reflexively out of concern that the adversary’s systems will act first.¶ Cyber operations are where this compression is already routine rather than prospective. Automated defensive responses operate at machine speed as standard practice, and the discovery and exploitation of software vulnerabilities is increasingly assisted by automated tooling. The consequence for crisis stability is that delegation in this domain tends to occur tacitly. Authority lapses instead of being handed over, because the pace of events leaves no interval in which a human could meaningfully intervene. A commander who retains nominal authority over a system whose recommendations arrive faster than they can be evaluated has delegated in practice while retaining authority on paper. Deterrence relies on deliberate signaling, calibrated responses, and the opportunity to pause, and each of these is reduced when the interval for judgment shrinks.¶ 3.6. Conditions shaping the strength of these mechanisms¶ The three mechanisms are not deterministic. Their strength depends on four conditions, each of which bears on all three.¶ Doctrinal clarity concerns whether states define and communicate how AI-enabled systems may be used. Public or private commitments to human authorization for critical actions, including a requirement for human confirmation before acting on AI-generated warning, reduce the scope for worst-case assumptions. Vague or secretive doctrine has the opposite effect, since ambiguity about AI’s role in nuclear command can lead one side to fear automated launch authority and act preemptively (Horowitz and Scharre Citation2018).¶ Transparency concerns what each side knows about the other’s systems and safeguards. Information exchange about autonomous deployments, notification of exercises, and channels for reporting anomalies reduce the chance that a technical fault is read as a hostile act (Horowitz and Scharre Citation2018). Ding and Jiang (Citation2025) note that opacity in military AI capabilities complicates threat assessment. Transparency carries a cost that is specific to this domain, however, since disclosing how a system works can assist an adversary seeking to manipulate it. States therefore face a tradeoff between reassurance and security that admits no clean resolution, and this tension recurs in Section 6.¶ Technological maturity concerns whether systems have been tested and validated before deployment. Mature systems are less prone to error, while systems fielded hastily under competitive pressure may misidentify threats or fail in unfamiliar conditions. Aguirre, Javorsky, and Tegmark (Citation2023) emphasize the dangers of false positives and misclassification, and J. Johnson (Citation2020) warns that “premature adoption of unsafe, error-prone, unverified, and unreliable AI technology” poses major risks. Maturity in this context includes resistance to adversarial manipulation, which is a distinct property from accuracy under benign conditions and is frequently not measured.¶ Strategic context concerns the political environment in which incidents are interpreted. In a high-tension crisis, for instance over Taiwan, a minor AI-driven anomaly may be read as hostile, while in a calmer setting with established crisis management mechanisms leaders may pause and verify. Existing norms, including mutual restraint regarding interference with nuclear command and control, moderate the effect. Without such norms, AI-enhanced capabilities are more likely to aggravate the security dilemma than to alleviate it.¶ 4. Evidence and approach¶ This study is based on a structured reading of open-source institutional documents. It is useful to state at the outset what that design can and cannot support, since the study addresses a subject where the most consequential evidence is unavailable.¶ Process tracing offers a well-developed standard for causal inference in single-case research, requiring evidence about the sequence of events within a case at a level of detail sufficient to distinguish between competing explanations of a particular outcome (Beach and Pedersen Citation2013; George and Bennett Citation2005). Meeting that standard for military AI and crisis stability would require access to internal deliberations, command-level decisions, and the operation of systems during actual crises. None of this is available. There have also been no great-power crises in which AI-enabled systems played a decisive role, so there is no outcome to trace backwards from. Presenting the analysis as process tracing would therefore claim an inferential warrant the evidence cannot supply.¶ The study is instead conducted as a plausibility probe (Eckstein Citation1975). It specifies mechanisms that could link AI adoption to crisis instability, establishes that these mechanisms are consistent with how the relevant institutions describe their own capabilities and concerns, and identifies the evidence that would strengthen or undercut them. The purpose is to establish that the mechanisms are worth investigating and to define what investigating them would require. Demonstrating that they have operated is beyond what this design can do.¶ The materials used are publicly available strategic documents, policy papers, official military doctrines, legislative hearing transcripts, and reports from policy institutes. The analysis draws on official publications including U.S. Department of Defense AI strategy documents and policy directives, the annual China Military Power Reports, Chinese state and defense policy texts, and assessments from bodies such as the Congressional Research Service, the National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence, the Government Accountability Office, and research institutions in both countries. For the cyber dimension of the argument, the analysis also draws on government cybersecurity advisories, which are institutional outputs in the same sense as doctrinal documents and carry the assessments of the agencies that issue them.¶ These documents are read as institutional outputs rather than as descriptions of events. What they provide is evidence of how organizations characterize risks, what commitments they are prepared to state publicly, where they identify tradeoffs, and how their stated priorities change over time. What they do not provide is evidence of what decision-makers believe privately or how they would act under pressure. The distinction matters throughout. A commitment to human authorization appearing in a policy directive is evidence that an organization has adopted a position and expects to be held to it. It is not evidence that the position would hold in a crisis, and the analysis does not treat it as such.¶ Selection followed three principles. Documents were included where they carried institutional authority, meaning official issuance or formal endorsement; where they bore directly on AI integration, command and control, crisis stability, escalation, or strategic signaling; and where their claims could be cross-checked against other document types and, where possible, against sources from the other country. Materials were excluded where they were speculative, duplicative, or lacked traceable provenance. Journalistic sources are used to corroborate or contextualize official statements, and carry no evidentiary weight on their own.¶ Three limitations bear on how the findings should be read. The first concerns asymmetry in the source base. U.S. institutional documents are more numerous, more detailed, and more likely to discuss internal disagreement than their Chinese counterparts, which creates a risk that U.S. positions appear better specified simply because they are better documented. Where the analysis makes claims about Chinese doctrinal preferences, these rest on a thinner evidentiary base and are stated with corresponding caution.¶ The second concerns the gap between declaration and practice. Public commitments serve multiple purposes, including reassurance of allies and management of domestic audiences, and there is no way to verify from open sources whether stated policies govern actual system design. This limitation cuts in a specific direction. Where the analysis identifies stabilizing commitments, those findings are weaker than they appear, since declaration is easier than compliance.¶ The third concerns the pace of technological change. Capabilities described in documents from even three or four years ago may no longer reflect what is deployed, and the classification boundary tends to move as capabilities mature, so the most consequential developments are the least visible. This constrains how far any conclusion drawn here should be projected forward, and it is a reason for framing the assessment in terms of indicators that can be revisited as circumstances change.¶ Finally, the mechanisms specified in Section 3 carry observable implications that would count against them. Attribution ambiguity would be weakened as a concern if states developed and shared verification methods allowing anomalies in AI-enabled systems to be diagnosed and communicated during a crisis. The data integrity mechanism would be weakened if AI-enabled ISR were consistently evaluated for resistance to adversarial manipulation rather than for accuracy alone, and if those evaluations were disclosed. The delegation mechanism would be weakened if command arrangements built mandatory verification intervals into decision processes and if states declared them. Section 6 assesses how far each of these has occurred, and the assessment offered there rests on that evidence, and holds only so far as the evidence does.¶ 5. AI integration and crisis risk in U.S.-china competition¶ This section examines how AI technologies integrated into military systems are shaping strategic perceptions, signaling, and stability between the United States and China. The purpose is to trace how competitive adoption pressures and doctrinal adaptation connect AI development to crisis dynamics through the three mechanisms identified above. The analysis is divided into three subsections, each examining one AI-enabled capability area: autonomous weapons systems, ISR technologies, and decision-support tools. In each case the discussion addresses both the capability itself and the cyber exposure it carries, since the two cannot be assessed separately.¶ 5.1. AWS and strategic stability¶ Both the United States and China have pursued AWS as part of their military modernization, reflecting a belief that AI-driven autonomy could confer decisive advantages. In Washington, the Third Offset Strategy launched in the mid-2010s prioritized next-generation technologies, notably artificial intelligence and autonomous systems, to preserve U.S. military superiority and strengthen deterrence (Department of Defense Citation2019). U.S. defense officials argued that leveraging autonomy, networking, and precision strike would “assure U.S. military superiority” while reducing the likelihood of war by bolstering conventional deterrence (Work Citation2015). The establishment of the Joint Artificial Intelligence Center in 2018 provided a Pentagon hub to accelerate AI-enabled capabilities across the services, signaling a commitment to operationalizing AI in a human-centered manner (Department of Defense Citation2019).¶ Policy on autonomy was formalized in DoD Directive 3000.09, originally issued in 2012 and updated in January 2023, which requires that autonomous and semi-autonomous weapon systems be designed to allow commanders and operators to exercise appropriate levels of human judgment over the use of force (Department of Defense Citation2023). The directive is the most concrete institutional commitment either state has made on this subject, and it is examined further below and in Section 6.¶ The Air Force’s Skyborg program (Citation2021) illustrates AWS development in practice. Skyborg is an autonomy project to field loyal wingman drones flying alongside piloted fighters, designed to extend sensor coverage and execute maneuvers rapidly in contested environments (Davis Citation2020). Policy dictates that human operators remain the ultimate decision-makers for lethal force, while the drones relay data in real time to support rapid judgments. By 2021, prototypes had demonstrated basic manned-unmanned teaming in flight tests. The Navy has pursued autonomous vessels including Sea Hunter, a 132-foot unmanned ship launched in 2016 and capable of months-long deployments without crew, conceived to trail submarines using onboard AI for navigation and tracking (Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency Citation2018). Autonomous maritime systems matter strategically because improved persistence and tracking shape perceptions of survivability, including in undersea competition.¶ China has responded with a drive for military intelligentization (智能化). Beijing views AI as central to closing legacy gaps and building a world-class military (Stokes Citation2024). In 2017, Xi called for the PLA to accelerate the development of military intelligentization, and by 2022 he urged speeding the development of unmanned, intelligent combat capabilities. China’s 2019 National Defense White Paper highlighted AI and autonomy as critical frontiers, and PLA publications since then discuss integrating AI across command, weapons, and support systems (Kania Citation2020). The Feihong-97A, an AI-enabled loyal wingman drone debuted at Airshow China in 2022, is designed to accompany the J-20 stealth fighter, and Chinese designers claim it can command swarms of smaller drones, acting as a coordinating platform for a networked swarm (McFadden Citation2024). In the maritime domain, the HSU-001 large unmanned underwater vehicle, showcased during the 2019 National Day parade, is a roughly five-meter robotic submarine built for long-endurance ISR and anti-submarine tasks, addressing a traditional PLA Navy weakness (Keller Citation2021).¶ Chinese military writings show close attention to U.S. developments. Chinese analysts frequently cite American concepts including the Third Offset and mosaic warfare, and Chinese research articles debate how to employ AI for systems destruction warfare, indicating plans to use autonomous systems to identify and strike the weak links of an adversary’s networked forces (Stokes Citation2024). The PLA’s emphasis on new domains and AI clusters is tied to a strategy of offsetting U.S. strengths by disrupting command and control. At least one of the two states explicitly conceives of AI-enabled advantage as something to be achieved by degrading the networks on which an opponent’s systems depend rather than by matching those systems platform for platform.¶ 5.1.1. Mechanism tracing¶ Autonomous systems introduce unpredictability. Because they can select targets and act without direct human input, they may behave in ways that diverge from commanders’ intent or adversaries’ expectations. A 2020 RAND wargame illustrates the danger, with AI-driven systems escalating a simulated crisis by reacting with unintended force to perceived threats (Tarallo Citation2020). Testing cannot eliminate such risks, since complex autonomous systems are prone to failures in contested environments and trials cannot replicate the fog of war. This concern is acute for China, where the PLA’s lack of recent combat experience limits opportunities to refine systems under stress (Kania Citation2020). Crises could therefore escalate through system error alone, with no deliberate decision behind them.¶ Cyber exposure compounds this problem in a specific way. The vulnerabilities of machine learning systems to deliberate manipulation are now documented in institutional terms. The U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology has published a taxonomy of adversarial machine learning that classifies attacks by the stage of the system lifecycle at which they occur, distinguishing poisoning attacks that corrupt training data from evasion attacks that manipulate inputs at deployment to change a model’s outputs (Vassilev et al. Citation2025). Real-world examples in that report include misclassification of road signs by vision systems. The military implication is that an autonomous platform’s anomalous behavior may be the intended result of adversary action.¶ This turns an interpretive problem into a strategic one. When a system behaves anomalously, the observing state faces at least three explanations: a fault in the system, adversary interference with its data or links, or a deliberate act by the operating state. Each implies a different response, and the evidence needed to distinguish them is not available on crisis timescales. The state that did not cause the anomaly faces the reciprocal difficulty of proving a negative, since demonstrating that one did not interfere with an opponent’s system requires disclosing knowledge of that system that would itself be alarming. This is the attribution problem familiar from cyber conflict (Lindsay Citation2015), relocated inside the operation of conventional platforms.¶ The opacity of AI decision-making also complicates signaling. Chinese analysts warn that AI increases the opacity of military capabilities, making it harder for the two states to assess each other’s intentions (Ding and Jiang Citation2025). A sudden re-routing of a U.S. drone swarm may be read as strategic signaling or as autonomous recalculation, and without clarity, worst-case assumptions prevail. Deployment of stealth drones such as the FH-97A carries similar ambiguity about whether the mission is offensive or routine. Conflict simulations indicate that autonomous systems sometimes ignore human de-escalation cues, including off-ramps (Tarallo Citation2020), so a conciliatory gesture may be lost while an automated action provokes. Official demonstrations compound the effect, since U.S. announcements intended to reassure domestic audiences may appear threatening in Beijing, and Chinese unmanned system tests may appear aggressive in Washington (Kania Citation2020).¶ Autonomous platforms also accelerate operations beyond human decision speed. Systems may act before humans intervene, compressing timelines and forcing decisions under pressure (Tarallo Citation2020). In a U.S.-China context involving sensitive assets, this could be destabilizing, particularly where conventional and nuclear decision loops blend (Klare and Liang Citation2024). In the RAND wargame, rapid cycles reduced opportunities for de-escalation, with attempts to pause overridden by the next autonomous move (Tarallo Citation2020). Faster offense may tempt states toward postures such as launch on warning.¶ Evidence from both countries indicates that AWS development is proceeding under competitive pressure and with limited mutual understanding. Directive 3000.09 provides a meaningful commitment on human judgment, and its limits should be noted. It is a unilateral policy with no bilateral counterpart, China has issued no equivalent public commitment, and, as discussed in Section 5.3, its scope excludes the domain where autonomous operation is most advanced. Given current incentives for speed and secrecy, the destabilizing pathways identified above are more likely to dominate in the near term, particularly through ambiguity and time compression. Stabilization is more plausible if both sides clarify human authorization thresholds and establish practical incident-clarification channels for autonomous system anomalies.¶ 5.2. AI-driven intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance¶ Artificial intelligence is transforming ISR by enabling faster data processing and autonomous analysis. Both states view AI-driven ISR as pivotal to information superiority. Machine learning algorithms can sift through streams of satellite imagery and drone video far more quickly than human analysts (Atherton Citation2018), and military analysts anticipate a system-of-systems approach in which AI networks link sensors to provide broad coverage and rapid targeting (Technology for Global Security & Center for Global Security Research Citation2019).¶ Better surveillance can bolster early warning and confidence in detecting adversary actions, reducing the likelihood of surprise (Zhang Citation2020). An intelligence advantage can also be destabilizing where it threatens an opponent’s deterrent forces or compresses decision times. A third possibility receives less attention and bears most directly on the argument here. The ISR architecture is itself a target, which raises a question alongside what each side can see: whether what it sees can be trusted.¶ The United States has pursued AI-enabled ISR as a priority. The Department of Defense’s 2018 Artificial Intelligence Strategy highlighted AI’s potential to transform intelligence analysis, and the Joint Artificial Intelligence Center was established the same year to scale AI across the services (Technology for Global Security & Center for Global Security Research Citation2019). Project Maven, launched in 2017, applied machine learning to full-motion video from drones, automating identification of objects in footage collected by MQ-9 Reaper and RQ-4 Global Hawk platforms. The tool accelerated imagery analysis, allowing analysts to process two to three times more footage in the same period (Atherton Citation2018), and demonstrated AI’s value in extracting intelligence from large datasets while prompting debate on ethical use (Atherton Citation2018).¶ China has made AI-driven ISR a cornerstone of modernization under intelligentization. The 2019 Defense White Paper stated that war is evolving in form toward informationized warfare, with intelligentized warfare on the horizon (State Council Information Office of the PRC Citation2019). The PLA has invested in ISR sensor architectures and data processing, including an expanding satellite constellation. The Gaofen series of high-resolution Earth observation satellites began launching in 2013, and China now operates dozens of reconnaissance satellites including the military Yaogan series. One U.S. Air Force study observes that extracting useful insight from the enormous quantities of raw data in China’s ISR network is likely an early priority for applying artificial intelligence. China’s Military-Civil Fusion strategy has mobilized leading technology firms to develop military AI tools for target recognition and image analysis. With Russian assistance, China is fielding a strategic ballistic missile early warning network, and Chinese experts have advocated using AI to improve sensor fusion and reduce false alarms (Zhang Citation2020). AI is expected to reinforce the reconnaissance-strike complex within China’s anti-access and area-denial posture by improving the tracking of adversary forces and cueing long-range precision strikes (Zhang Citation2020).¶ 5.2.1. Mechanism tracing¶ Improved surveillance and faster analysis can reduce uncertainty in crises. If AI enables China to reliably detect an incoming attack, Beijing may feel less pressure to use its nuclear forces early. China has long been anxious about false negatives, meaning a missed first strike, and applying AI to its early warning systems could mitigate fears of a surprise nuclear attack, improving crisis stability by assuring Beijing that it would notice a major threat in time (Zhang Citation2020). AI tools can also filter noise from large intelligence datasets, potentially reducing false alarms.¶ These stabilizing effects are conditional on the integrity of the data, and open-source evidence indicates that the condition is contested. In February 2024, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, together with the National Security Agency and the Federal Bureau of Investigation, assessed that PRC state-sponsored actors had pre-positioned themselves on the networks of U.S. critical infrastructure organizations in order to enable disruption or destruction of services in the event of a major crisis or conflict, with confirmed compromises across communications, energy, transportation, and water sectors (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, National Security Agency, & Federal Bureau of Investigation Citation2024). The advisory noted a shift in PRC cyber activity from espionage toward pre-positioning for disruption. Two points follow for this analysis. The first is that access placed in advance for use during a crisis is exactly the pattern that generates ambiguity, since the same access supports collection and disruption and the target cannot determine which purpose is intended (Buchanan Citation2017). The second is that the reciprocal expectation is now established. Each side plans on the assumption that its networks are contested, and each has reason to believe the same of the other.¶ A compromised ISR pipeline does not announce itself. Where an adversary can influence what a fusion system sees, the system continues to produce confident assessments, and it produces them faster than the analytic processes that once caught errors. This is a different failure from the false positives discussed in the AWS literature, because an operator who distrusts a sensor seeks corroboration while an operator who trusts a manipulated one does not. The stabilizing potential of AI-enabled ISR therefore rests on an assumption about data integrity that neither state can currently verify, and the greater a state’s confidence in its ISR, the more consequential a successful manipulation becomes.¶ Several destabilizing pathways follow independently of manipulation. AI-augmented sensors may enable tracking of systems previously considered secure, including mobile launchers and ballistic missile submarines. Networked drones guided by AI might shadow mobile launchers or hunt submarines, eroding the concealment that underwrites second-strike capability (J. Johnson Citation2020). If either state came to believe its retaliatory forces were vulnerable to detection, pressure to preempt in a crisis would grow, and even the perception of an intelligence imbalance can be destabilizing. AI-enhanced conventional capabilities could therefore exacerbate the risk of inadvertent escalation by undermining nuclear force survivability, particularly where nuclear and conventional assets are entangled (J. Johnson Citation2020).¶ Automation of analysis compresses the decision cycle. If a system flags an anomaly in seconds, commanders may feel compelled to act. The PLA’s exploration of automation for launch on warning, intended to avoid missing an incoming strike, might reduce Chinese fears of false negatives while intensifying U.S. concerns about false positives (Zhang Citation2020).¶ The race for ISR superiority is itself destabilizing. Each side has incentives to invest in counter-ISR measures, from network attacks to anti-satellite weapons. These incentives are not symmetrical in their escalatory implications. Cyber counter-ISR is attractive because it is deniable, reversible, and available below the threshold of armed attack, which makes it more likely to be used and harder to interpret when it is. An intrusion into an ISR network may be preparation for wartime disruption, ongoing collection, or an attempt to assess what the adversary can see, and the target cannot distinguish among these. The deniability that makes cyber counter-ISR attractive in peacetime is what makes it dangerous in a crisis. Attacking ISR assets can be highly escalatory, since a blinding attack on early warning satellites might be read as preparation for a nuclear strike. Under current conditions the destabilizing pathways are more likely to dominate, because survivability fears and counter-ISR incentives reinforce worst-case inference. Stabilization is more plausible if early warning automation is paired with verification safeguards and crisis communication arrangements that reduce incentives to strike ISR assets preemptively.¶ 5.3. AI-enabled strategic decision-support systems¶ Strategic decision-support systems are analytical platforms designed to aid military and political leaders in high-stakes decisions. They integrate data from sensors, intelligence, and communications and transform it into inputs for command and control networks (GAO Citation2025). AI-enabled systems sift information, identify patterns, and propose courses of action, affecting the speed of decision-making in complex environments (Lin-Greenberg Citation2020). Both states are integrating such tools into strategic planning and command processes (Stokes Citation2024).¶ The United States has pursued AI-enabled decision-support as part of command-and-control modernization. Following the establishment of the Joint Artificial Intelligence Center in 2018 (Barnett Citation2019), the Combined Joint All-Domain Command and Control initiative sought to integrate sensors, shooters, and decision-makers, using AI to enhance decision speed (GAO Citation2025). A GAO report emphasized the Department’s pivot toward automated and scalable decision-making tools to manage operational data streams (GAO Citation2025). A 2019 Air Force joint exercise featured an AI system that completed a targeting cycle by autonomously recommending sensor retasking and engagement actions, compressing reaction time substantially (Lin-Greenberg Citation2020). Congressional oversight, including mandates in the 2020 National Defense Authorization Act, has stressed responsible integration and transparency (Barnett Citation2019; GAO Citation2025).¶ China has prioritized AI-enabled decision-support under intelligentization (Dahm Citation2020). The 2017 State Council AI Development Plan advocated advances in defense-related intelligent command systems (Dahm Citation2020). PLA doctrine values AI for systems destruction warfare, targeting an adversary’s communication, sensor, and decision-making nodes (Dahm Citation2020; Stokes Citation2024), and Chinese strategic literature discusses AI’s potential to execute cyber-electronic warfare and command-level disruption rapidly (Dahm Citation2020).¶ 5.3.1. Mechanism tracing¶ AI compresses decision windows by accelerating threat detection and option analysis. Faster decisions may offer tactical advantages while forcing leaders into hurried actions, increasing escalation risk (Klare and Liang Citation2024). In crises, the pace of AI-driven decision cycles could reduce opportunities for diplomatic engagement and deliberation.¶ The cyber domain provides the clearest evidence that machine-speed operation is already current. DARPA’s AI Cyber Challenge, conducted between 2023 and 2025 and concluded at DEF CON in August 2025, required competing systems to find and patch software vulnerabilities with human intervention prohibited. In the final round, seven autonomous systems analyzed challenge projects derived from critical infrastructure software over roughly 143 hours of unsupervised operation, and in addition to the synthetic vulnerabilities introduced for scoring they discovered eighteen previously unknown flaws in real open-source code (Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency Citation2025; Kapko Citation2025). The competition was defensive in purpose and its results were disclosed responsibly. The capability it demonstrated is not intrinsically defensive, since finding an exploitable flaw is the same operation whether the finder intends to patch it or use it.¶ This bears on delegation in a way the existing literature has not addressed. Directive 3000.09, the sole binding U.S. policy on autonomy in weapon systems, states explicitly that it does not apply to autonomous or semi-autonomous cyberspace capabilities (Department of Defense Citation2023). The domain in which autonomous operation is furthest advanced is therefore the domain excluded from the principal governance instrument, and the exclusion is deliberate, reflecting the impracticality of human authorization at the speeds at which network operations occur.¶ The consequence is that delegation in this domain tends to occur without being decided. Automated defensive response is routine, and a defensive action that alters or disables a system on an adversary’s network is difficult to distinguish from an offensive one from the receiving end. Where two states operate automated systems that respond to each other’s activity, an exchange can develop without either having authorized it, and each side’s automated response constitutes evidence to the other of hostile intent. Nothing in the open record indicates that either state has established procedures for pausing such an exchange, and the absence is consistent with the technical difficulty of doing so.¶ Opacity in AI systems can also exacerbate mistrust. Complex algorithms often obscure the rationale behind recommendations, heightening uncertainty about the intentions behind AI-informed actions (J. Johnson Citation2020). States may read aggressive intent into actions that reflect algorithmic processing.¶ Increased delegation reduces human oversight. Delegating decisions to algorithms during crises risks unintended escalation through automation bias or erroneous outputs (J. Johnson Citation2020; Klare and Liang Citation2024). The more consequential form of delegation may be the informal kind. A commander who retains formal authority over a system whose outputs arrive faster than they can be evaluated has delegated in substance while retaining authority on paper, and this arrangement is compatible with every existing human-in-the-loop commitment.¶ Given competitive incentives to accelerate decision cycles, decision-support systems currently tilt toward destabilization through time compression, opacity, and automation bias. Stabilization is more plausible if doctrine and design preserve meaningful human verification time at critical thresholds, if crisis procedures include explicit slow-down checks when AI outputs drive high-stakes decisions, and if the governance gap covering autonomous cyber operations is addressed.¶ 6. Managing the risk: conditions, governance, and assessment¶ Section 3 specified four conditions determining how strongly the three mechanisms operate. This section assesses how far each condition is currently satisfied, examines how policymakers and strategic analysts have framed and attempted to manage these risks, and offers a bounded assessment of where the balance currently sits.¶ 6.1. The four conditions assessed¶ Doctrinal clarity is partial and asymmetric. The United States has issued a public policy on autonomy in weapon systems requiring appropriate levels of human judgment over the use of force (Department of Defense Citation2023), which is the most specific commitment either state has made. China has issued no equivalent public doctrine, and its authoritative statements on intelligentization describe ambition rather than constraint. The asymmetry itself carries risk, since a state that has published its constraints and receives nothing comparable in return has reason to doubt whether restraint is reciprocated.¶ Transparency is low and structurally difficult to raise. Neither state discloses how AI systems function within command arrangements, and the tradeoff identified in Section 3 explains why. Disclosure sufficient to reassure an adversary about a system’s safeguards would also assist an adversary seeking to manipulate it. The obstacle is genuine, and it distinguishes military AI from earlier subjects of confidence-building, where verification and security were less directly opposed. The implication is that transparency measures for this domain must be designed around the tension.¶ Technological maturity is difficult to assess from open sources and is unlikely to be uniformly high. Competitive pressure creates incentives to field systems before validation is complete, and the relevant form of maturity here includes resistance to deliberate manipulation, which is a distinct property from accuracy under benign conditions (Vassilev et al. Citation2025). Public accounts of military AI evaluation focus on performance, and no evidence in the open record indicates that either state requires adversarial robustness as a fielding criterion.¶ Strategic context is unfavorable. The relationship is characterized by limited military-to-military communication and by documented mutual intrusion into networks supporting critical functions (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, National Security Agency, & Federal Bureau of Investigation Citation2024), against a background of contested claims in the Taiwan Strait and the South China Sea. Under these conditions, the interpretive charity that would allow an anomaly to be read as a fault is in short supply.¶ 6.2. How the risks are being understood and managed¶ Policymakers in both countries have recognized these risks, and the response has been concentrated in declaratory and multilateral instruments. Verification and bilateral crisis machinery remain largely absent.¶ The most significant bilateral step came in November 2024, when President Biden and President Xi affirmed the need to maintain human control over the decision to use nuclear weapons and stressed the need to develop military AI prudently and responsibly (White House Citation2024). This was the first joint statement of its kind between the two states, and it followed the first formal bilateral talks on AI, held in Geneva in May 2024. Its significance should be neither dismissed nor overstated. It establishes a shared declaratory position on the single most consequential application, and it carries no verification provision, no definition of what human control requires in practice, and no scope beyond nuclear use decisions.¶ Multilateral efforts have proceeded on parallel and largely non-intersecting tracks. The United States launched the Political Declaration on Responsible Military Use of Artificial Intelligence and Autonomy at the REAIM summit in February 2023, a non-binding framework covering auditability, testing, and human accountability in the chain of command, now endorsed by more than fifty states (U.S. Department of State Citation2023). China has not endorsed it, and abstained on the first United Nations General Assembly resolution addressing autonomy in weapon systems. China has instead advanced its own framework, the Global AI Governance Initiative announced in October 2023 and circulated at the United Nations, emphasizing state sovereignty and a United Nations-centered process, followed by a Global AI Governance Action Plan in July 2025 (United Nations General Assembly Citation2023). The two frameworks proceed from different premises about where authority over such rules should sit, which limits convergence even where their substantive content overlaps.¶ On the cyber dimension, the United Nations Open-Ended Working Group on security in the use of information and communications technologies concluded its mandate in July 2025 with a consensus final report establishing a permanent mechanism for continued discussion. Reaching consensus at all was an achievement under prevailing conditions, and the substantive disagreements that have characterized these negotiations for two decades were not resolved.¶ Strategic analysts have been ahead of policymakers in identifying the specific risk this article addresses. The scholarship reviewed in Section 2 established well before these initiatives that information integrity, attribution difficulty, and entanglement generate escalation risk independently of firepower (Acton Citation2018; Buchanan Citation2017; Futter Citation2018). The governance response has not tracked that analysis. Existing instruments address autonomy in the use of force and the conduct of cyber operations as separate subjects, and the risk identified here arises at their intersection.¶ 6.3. What the measures leave out¶ 6.3.1. Three gaps follow from the preceding survey¶ The first is the exclusion of autonomous cyber operations. Directive 3000.09 states that it does not apply to autonomous or semi-autonomous cyberspace capabilities (Department of Defense Citation2023), and no comparable instrument covers them. The domain where autonomous operation is furthest advanced and where machine-tempo interaction is already routine sits outside the principal governance framework, and the exclusion reflects the practical difficulty of requiring human authorization at network speeds. That difficulty is real, and it does not make the resulting gap less consequential.¶ The second is the absence of incident machinery. Nothing in the open record indicates that either state has established a channel for clarifying anomalies in AI-enabled systems during a crisis. Given the three-way ambiguity described in Section 5, where an anomaly may reflect fault, manipulation, or intent, the absence of such a channel means that the interpretation most likely to be adopted under time pressure is the one that assumes hostile action.¶ The third is the gap between declaration and verification. Every commitment surveyed above is declaratory. As noted in Section 4, declaration is easier than compliance, and no mechanism exists by which either state could demonstrate adherence or detect its absence. This bears asymmetrically on the assessment offered below, since the stabilizing evidence carries less weight than the destabilizing evidence.¶ Meeting these gaps would require extending existing frameworks, and no new institution is needed. Candidate measures include declaratory commitments covering autonomous cyber operations, notification arrangements for anomalies in systems supporting early warning, and agreement on evaluation standards for adversarial robustness in systems informing high-consequence decisions. These would be modest steps, and each is compatible with the tension between transparency and security identified above, since none requires disclosing how a system works in order to state what it will not be permitted to do.¶ 6.4. Assessment¶ The analysis above implies a conditional but directional assessment. Under current U.S.-China competitive conditions, the balance of indicators leans toward destabilization pressures more than managed stabilization. The claim rests on the observation that competitive adoption currently reinforces the pathways described in Section 5 while the measures capable of containing them remain declaratory. Autonomous systems increase uncertainty and ambiguity under limited transparency, AI-enabled ISR creates survivability fears and counter-ISR incentives while depending on data integrity that neither side can verify, and decision-support tools compress deliberation time and intensify automation dependence.¶ The assessment is offered with a stated limit. Given the pace of change described in Section 4, it characterizes present conditions and should not be read forward. Three observable indicators can help evaluate whether dynamics are moving toward stabilization or destabilization. First, whether AI-enabled ISR and targeting are increasingly framed, explicitly or implicitly, as counterforce-enabling capabilities that erode confidence in survivability. Second, whether crisis decision processes become more automation-dependent, including tacit delegation and automation bias, as actors seek to match tempo. Third, whether the rivalry produces credible confidence-building measures such as incident channels for AI anomalies and commitments to human authorization that extend beyond nuclear use decisions. Movement on the first two indicators without progress on the third is consistent with a worsening crisis stability environment even absent deliberate escalation intent.¶ One further consideration bears on how AI affects the underlying logic of deterrence. If AI-enabled systems allow one side to locate and hold at risk the other’s retaliatory forces, the mutual vulnerability on which deterrence rests is weakened, producing an AI security dilemma in which each state, fearing its deterrent could be negated, feels pressure to advance its own capabilities (J. Johnson Citation2023). The argument developed here suggests a second and less examined route to the same outcome. Confidence in a deterrent can be eroded without any change in the physical balance, if a state comes to doubt whether the systems reporting on that balance can be trusted. That possibility is consistent with the definition of strategic stability set out in Section 3, which already contemplates unconventional means, and it has received less attention than the counterforce pathway.¶ 7. Conclusion¶ This article asked how the cyber exposure of AI-enabled military systems shapes crisis stability between the United States and China. It specified three mechanisms through which that
through autonomous weapons systems, AI-enabled ISR, and decision-support tools

. The claim connecting the three is that the escalation risks associated with military AI arise mainly from the contested networks and data on which those systems depend. The autonomy of any individual platform is a secondary source of risk. On that reading, the reliability of a military AI system is something an adversary can work to undermine, and the strategic consequences follow from that fact.¶ The article does not offer a verdict on whether AI will stabilize or destabilize the relationship. Given the pace of technological change and the limits of the available evidence, no such verdict is currently available. What the analysis supports is narrower. Under present competitive conditions, the pathways generating risk are being reinforced while the measures capable of containing them remain declaratory. Three findings underpin that assessment. The principal U.S. policy on autonomy in weapon systems excludes autonomous cyberspace capabilities, leaving the domain where autonomous operation is furthest advanced outside the governing instrument. No channel exists for clarifying anomalies in AI-enabled systems during a crisis, which means the ambiguity identified in Section 5 would be resolved under time pressure by inference, with no means of inquiry available. And every commitment surveyed is declaratory, with no mechanism by which adherence could be demonstrated or its absence detected. Section 6 specifies three indicators by which this assessment can be revisited.¶ The theoretical contribution is a modest one. Scholarship on cyber conflict established that ambiguity, intrusion, and contested information generate escalation risk independently of firepower, and scholarship on military AI has concentrated on autonomy and speed. Reading the two together suggests a route to eroded deterrence that has received less attention than the counterforce pathway. Confidence in a deterrent can weaken without any change in the physical balance of forces, if a state comes to doubt whether the systems reporting on that balance can be trusted.¶ The policy implication follows directly from the gaps identified in Section 6.

, and none requires a state to disclose how its systems work in order to state what those systems will not be permitted to do.¶ The analysis has limitations. Reliance on open-source materials means that developments related to nuclear command and control and to classified deployments remain opaque, and strategic intent behind AI adoption is difficult to measure from institutional documents. The source base is also asymmetric, since U.S. documents are more numerous and more detailed than their Chinese counterparts, so claims about Chinese doctrinal preferences rest on thinner evidence. The findings are suggestive, and nothing more than that is claimed for them. Although this article focuses on narrow AI because that is what is currently being integrated into ISR, autonomous systems, and decision-support architectures, elite and public debate often centers on the possibility of AGI. Such expectations can raise the perceived cost of falling behind even without imminent realization, and the analysis here treats them as a factor shaping perceptions, and makes no forecast.¶ Several lines of further work follow. Wargames could build deliberate manipulation of AI-enabled systems into scenario design, so that players face an anomaly whose cause is genuinely undetermined. What they do under that condition would test the attribution ambiguity described here. Comparative work across other dyads would also be valuable. Russia and NATO, or India and Pakistan, differ both in strategic culture and in how far their command architectures depend on networks, and that variation offers leverage on the conditions specified in Section 3. Should a crisis involving AI-enabled systems occur, it would supply the within-case evidence this design could not reach.¶ For policymakers the practical question is a narrow one: whether two states running opaque systems inside each other’s networks can work out why a system behaved as it did, and communicate that answer to each other, while there is still time for it to change anything.
